newsitem.title: USA: Ahmanson says Great Western/Washington Mutual may be delayed.
newsitem.headline: Ahmanson says Great Western/Washington Mutual may be delayed.

text.p: H.F. Ahmanson and Co. persisted in its hostile $6.8 billion bid for Great Western Financial Corp. Monday and asserted a friendly $6.9 billion takeover by rival bidder Washington Mutual Inc. would face regulatory issues and delays.

Ahmanson, the Irwindale, Calif.-based parent of Home Savings of America, said Washington Mutual and Great Western should disclose to shareholders some outstanding issues relating to Washington Mutual's ability to qualify as a so-called unitary thrift holding company after the merger.
Unitary thrift charters enable banks to be involved in all sorts of businesses, whereas multiple thrift charters or standard bank charters face certain limitations.
Ahmanson said by merging Great Western into Washington Mutual's American Savings Bank unit, Washington Mutual will no longer qualify as a unitary thrift holding company.
Ahmanson said it believed Washington Mutual could face delays and may be forced to sell some of its non-banking businesses, which could affect underlying earnings, in order to complete the deal.

Ahmanson launched a hostile bid in February for Chatsworth, Calif.-based Great Western and has been fighting to complete the deal despite Great Western's rejection of the offer and its merger agreement, announced March 6, with white knight Washington Mutual.
The merger would create the largest thrift in the United States, with assets of about $86 billion.

Washington Mutual said Monday that Ahmanson's statements were a blatant attempt to mislead investors regarding the status of Washington Mutual's Office of Thrift Supervision application for approval to merge with Great Western.
Agency spokesman William Fulwider said the office was reviewing the merger applications and declined further comment.
A Great Western attorney said, "There's no multiple holding company problem in the Washington Mutual transaction. Basically, it's a non-issue."
Smith Barney analyst Thomas O'Donnell said all the legal wranglings would not make or break the deal.
"My view is the premium will determine the deal. The market will determine the battle, and I think Washington Mutual will get Great Western unless Ahmanson sweetens its bid," said O'Donnell.

Analysts said investors are favouring Seattle-based Washington Mutual's bid since it was a friendly transaction endorsed by Great Western's board and because of Washington Mutual Chairman Kerry Killinger's reputation and success in executing acquisitions, a total of 22 in the last 10 years.

After Great Western and Washington Mutual agreed to merge in March, Ahmanson raised its bid and is now offering up to 1.2 of its shares for each Great Western share, while Washington Mutual's deal calls for an exchange of 0.9 of a share for each Great Western share.
Based on Monday's prices, Ahmanson's bid was valued at $48.90 a share, or about $6.8 billion, while Washington Mutual's bid was worth $49.50 a share, or about $6.9 billion.
Ahmanson was unchanged at $40.75 while Great Western fell 75 cents to $47.75, both on the New York Stock Exchange. Washington Mutual fell 62.5 cents to $55 on Nasdaq.
